passage:
In their village outside Malerkotla, Rashid, nineteen, was known for his temper. He had broken a plastic chair at a wedding over a parking argument, and the elders shook their heads when he passed. His sister Zeenat was the one who dragged him to the kabaddi ground behind the government school. "You want to fight? Fight with rules," she said.
The coach put him in as a raider. Rashid charged, got tackled, came up furious, and the coach said, "Good. Now breathe, and do it smarter." Every evening after that he trained until dark: footwork, breath-holding, the "kabaddi-kabaddi" chant on one breath.
At the district tournament, a defender shoved him hard after the whistle. Rashid's jaw tightened. Then he turned, walked back to his line, and scored on the next raid.

qa.q: What position did the coach give Rashid?
qa.a: The coach put him in as a raider.

qa.q: What does Rashid's tightened jaw after the late shove suggest, and why did he walk back?
qa.a: His old anger flared, but training had given it a place with rules, so he chose to spend it on the next raid instead of a fight.

qa.q: Which choice of Zeenat's set things in motion, and why did it work?
qa.a: Taking him to the kabaddi ground with 'Fight with rules', which honoured his intensity instead of just telling him to calm down.

qa.q: How might the village elders see Rashid after the district tournament?
qa.a: They might start seeing a disciplined player instead of the young man who broke a chair, and shake their heads less.

grounding: A hot-tempered young man in a Punjab village finds kabaddi, where his intensity is welcomed within rules and channelled rather than denied.

passage:
At his college in Lyon, Nour had been called into the dean's office twice for shouting matches in class. He argued like he was drowning. His friend Selin, who ran the debating society, finally said, "Come on Thursday. You get seven minutes to destroy an argument, and nobody calls security."
The first week, he interrupted the other side and lost points. The judge said, "Passion is fine. Rudeness loses." So he practised: timing his rebuttals with a stopwatch, writing counter-arguments on index cards, waiting for his turn with his hands pressed flat on the table.
By spring he was the society's fiercest speaker, and its most polite. After one final, his opponent shook his hand. "You're terrifying," she said, "in a good way."

qa.q: What did Nour write his counter-arguments on?
qa.a: Index cards.

qa.q: Why might Nour have 'argued like he was drowning' before he joined the society?
qa.a: Nour seems to have felt frustrated and angry with nowhere for that intensity to go, so it burst out in shouting matches until debating gave it rules and a purpose.

qa.q: What turning point came after his first week of debating?
qa.a: Hearing 'Passion is fine. Rudeness loses' and choosing to practise timing and waiting his turn, which kept his fire but gave it discipline.

qa.q: How might Selin feel watching Nour become the fiercest and most polite speaker?
qa.a: Selin would likely feel proud and relieved that the invitation worked, seeing a friend's temper turn into a strength. 👍

grounding: A young man in France with a fierce temper finds debating, where his intensity is welcomed within rules.

passage:
At the police sports club boxing hall in Ludhiana, Kishore was the new trainee who hit the bag like it had insulted his family. He had joined because the college warned him after a fight in the canteen. Coach Gurleen watched for a week, then stopped him mid-combination. "You have power. Now earn the right to use it."
She gave him rules: gloves touch before every spar, no punches after the bell, ten minutes of skipping before he could even look at a partner. Kishore hated the skipping. He did it anyway.
At the club championship he still fought fiercely, but when his opponent stumbled, Kishore stepped back and waited for the referee. Gurleen nodded once from the corner. That night he ate dinner with the team instead of alone.

qa.q: Why had Kishore joined the boxing club?
qa.a: The college warned him after a fight in the canteen.

qa.q: Why might Kishore have hated the skipping but done it anyway?
qa.a: He wanted to hit, not wait, but he seemed to want Gurleen's respect and the right to use his power even more.

qa.q: Which of Coach Gurleen's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Naming his power as something to earn and giving clear rules, which honoured his drive while teaching control.

qa.q: How might his opponent have felt when Kishore stepped back after the stumble?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, facing a fierce fighter who still played fair.

grounding: A young man with a fierce temper joins a boxing club where a coach channels his intensity through rules.

passage:
Dear Pankaj,
Remember the Class 12 fight near the canteen, when I nearly got thrown out? You'll laugh. I've joined the debating society at college.
First session I was a disaster. I shouted, I pointed, I called the other speaker "clueless". The adjudicator, a quiet final-year student called Shreya, docked me three points and said, "You're strong. Aim it at the argument, not the person."
That stuck. There are rules: seven minutes, a bell, points of information, no insults. Inside those rules, all my heat is actually useful. Last week I took apart a motion on fuel prices so hard the room clapped, and nobody got hurt.
I still get the rush, the same one that used to end in fists. Now it ends in a scoresheet. Ma says she finally has a son she can boast about. We're in the inter-college semis on Saturday.
Come and watch if you're in Bhopal.
Hrithik

qa.q: How many points did the adjudicator dock Hrithik in the first session?
qa.a: Three points.

qa.q: What does the rush Hrithik still feels suggest about his temper?
qa.a: The fierce drive hasn't gone away; it is the same energy that used to end in fists, now used inside rules where it is welcome.

qa.q: What turning point helped Hrithik use his intensity well?
qa.a: Shreya's advice to aim it at the argument, not the person; with a bell, time limits and no insults, his heat became a skill.

qa.q: How might Pankaj, who saw the Class 12 fight, read this letter?
qa.a: Pankaj may be surprised and glad to see that the friend who nearly got thrown out now wins applause with the same fire.

grounding: Shows a young man with a fierce temper finding debating, where his intensity is welcomed inside rules and channelled rather than denied.

passage:
You want the story for the college magazine, Pooja? Fine, but it's not a pretty one.
First year, I was that guy. Someone bumped my bike, I'd be in his face. I got a warning letter from the proctor after a shouting match in the parking lot. My Abbu came all the way from Barabanki and didn't say a word on the bus home. That was worse than any shouting.
Then Coach Verma saw me arguing at the canteen and said, "You have lungs and legs. Come to kabaddi." First practice, I charged like a bull and got tackled flat. Coach said, "Anger makes you fast. Rules make you win." Hold your breath, one raid, touch and return, no shoving after the whistle.
Now when I feel that heat, I save it for the raid. We won the zonal last month. Write that I still get angry, Pooja. I just know where it goes now. And put my name right: Irfan, with an f.

qa.q: What did Coach Verma say at the first practice?
qa.a: "Anger makes you fast. Rules make you win."

qa.q: Why did Abbu's silence on the bus feel worse to Irfan than shouting?
qa.a: It showed how deeply disappointed Abbu was, and Irfan felt the weight of that more than any scolding.

qa.q: What choice helped Irfan most, and why?
qa.a: Saying yes to kabaddi; its rules, like one breath per raid, touch and return, and no shoving after the whistle, gave his heat a place where it was welcome 👍

qa.q: What might Abbu see in Irfan now, compared with the day of the warning letter?
qa.a: Abbu might see a son whose fire hasn't been crushed but is used with discipline, and feel proud instead of ashamed.

grounding: Illustrates a young man with a hot temper who channels it into kabaddi, where intensity is honoured inside clear rules.
